title: What's a gap year anyway?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain the gap year: a year off, typically between high school and college (or after college), spent traveling, volunteering, or immersing in other cultures. They cover its origins in the 1960s and 1970s British and Australian hippie-trail and volunteer programs (Project Trust, Graham Turner's Top Deck bus tours, Tony and Maureen Wheeler's Lonely Planet), the 1990s growth of gap-year travel and the gap year dot com site, and the cheap flight coupons of the 1980s and 90s. They discuss benefits such as reduced burnout, maturity, clearer career direction, and better college performance (studies from Middlebury College, UNC, and Australia), along with college deferral and programs at Princeton and Florida State. Criticisms covered include privilege, voluntourism and neo-colonialism, and parental worries about cost and falling behind. Also included is an off-topic banter about airline seating, and listener mail about Cockney rhyming slang from Australian cricket players.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to gap years
segments.summary: Hosts open with show tour plugs and banter, then introduce gap years as a year off between high school and college, and Josh explains his own misunderstanding of the term.

segments.title: What a gap year is and who takes them
segments.summary: Hosts describe gap years as a time for maturing, volunteering, travel and cultural immersion, note they are popular in Britain and Australia far more than the United States, and share personal college-delay stories.
topics: gap year popularity UK Australia US

segments.title: Burnout and high school pressure
segments.summary: The hosts discuss burnout as a reason for gap years, including studies of student mental health, and contrast their own easier high school experience with today's competitive high schools and helicopter parenting.

segments.title: Gap year statistics and Malia Obama
segments.summary: Hosts cite UK and US participation rates from 2011 and discuss how Malia Obama's gap year through the Where There Be Dragons program brought attention to the idea in the US.

segments.title: Origins of the gap year in the 1960s and 1970s
segments.summary: The hosts trace the gap year to 1960s Britain and the Beat generation, Nicholas McLean Bristol's Project Trust, the hippie trail overland to India and Asia, and Graham Turner's double decker bus tours through Top Deck Travel.

segments.title: Lonely Planet and the alternative travel industry
segments.summary: The hosts describe Tony and Maureen Wheeler's overland trip and book Asia on the Cheap, which became the first Lonely Planet title, and the rise of an alternative, do-it-yourself travel industry, including Gap Activity Projects.

segments.title: Travel agents, cheap flights and seat-swapping tangent
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the Internet affected travel agents and the cheap backpacker flights of the 1980s and 1990s such as Air Hitch, then digress into airline seating preferences and asking to swap seats.

segments.title: Gap year growth in the 1990s and gap year dot com
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1990s growth of gap years in the UK, the gap year dot com website as an early social media site for gap years, and transition to a break.

segments.title: Benefits of gap years for students and parents
segments.summary: The hosts reassure parents, cite a Wall Street Journal story about a woman who learned she hated solar work, discuss colleges like Princeton and Florida State that support gap years, and report study results from Middlebury, UNC, and Australia on grades and career satisfaction.
topics: Florida State University gap year financial aid

segments.title: Criticisms, voluntourism and cost
segments.summary: The hosts discuss concerns about rustiness and falling behind, privilege, neo-colonialism and voluntourism citing Pippa Biddle's critique, how to plan a gap year with structure, and low-cost options like AmeriCorps and City Year.

segments.title: Listener mail: Cockney rhyming slang
segments.summary: Listener Tom McGlasson in Sydney writes about rhyming slang used among Australian cricket players, after an earlier episode on Cockney rhyming slang.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask listeners to follow on social media and email, and sign off.
